## 1) Chart type
A **composite visualization** combining:
- **Two horizontal bar charts** at the top
- **One tabular heatmap / highlighted table** at the bottom

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **multi-panel layout**:
  - Left panel: horizontal bars by **state**
  - Right panel: horizontal bars by **age at entry**
  - Bottom panel: **table** of occupations with two numeric columns
- No stacking is used.
- No faceting in the strict repeated-scale sense, but it functions as **separate panels/small sections** for different variables.
- Color highlighting is used to emphasize selected values/cells.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Row position / y-position in left horizontal bar chart; text label |
| DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in left chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Age at entry | Ordinal (discrete numeric categories shown as ages 0–15) | Row position / y-position in right horizontal bar chart; text label |
| Percent of DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in right chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Occupation | Categorical/nominal | Row position in bottom table; text label |
| DACA-eligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in left numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| DACA-ineligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in right numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| Highlight/emphasis status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (yellow vs blue in bars; shaded cells in table) |

I notice that the majority of DACA beneficiaries come from California and Texas. Also, the larger percent of entry at 9.7% comes at the age of 3 with percentages going down after that age I also notice in the second table that the majority of DACA eligible workers work in fairly good paying jobs with not as much physical labor such as in sales or in an office space while DACA ineligible workers work in more physically demanding or dangerous jobs such as Construction and Fishing. I wonder why California and Texas have more beneficiaries. Maybe it is because of its proximity to a foreign country(Mexico). I also wonder why the age of 3 is the largest age of entry. Maybe it could be because its the age when they start going to school and parents want them to have a life full of potential. Also being ineligible might hinder one from getting a high paying, minimal physical laboring job.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of  “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  Today’s graphs show who are the  'Dreamers' -- Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients.  From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  Plus, share with us a catchy headline. On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
(The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released tomorrow -- Thursday, Dec. 6 with moderation on Wednesday, December 12.  The topic -- fastest running shoes.)

raw_comment:
I noticed that California and Texas have the largest number of DACA children. This makes sense, since America's largest influx of immigrants are coming from Mexico and Central America as of late. I also observed that 3-year-olds make up the largest individual group benefitted by this program. This makes sense for families who want to immigrate ASAP but can't deal with the needs of a baby. Especially in illegal cases- toddlers can walk on their own if needed and can be reasoned with if their parents need them to stay quiet.
I wonder why these particular states are pictured on this graph- past New York they seem to be almost random. Does DACA have better/larger facilities in these states? Did their governments make a special agreement?
My catchy headline would be: "DACA Dreamers: What really happens to America's young immigrants?"

raw_comment:
I noticed that the largest number of DACA participants come from the two most populous border states of California and Texas. California is almost 100k more than Texas and Texas is more than double Illinois. This is, however, unsurprising because they are on the border and they both have large economies that can offer plenty of job opportunities. I also noticed that the largest age group at entry was at 3 yrs, but between 1 yr and 7 yrs the percentage remained fairly steady, but starts to steadily decline after age 7. 

I wonder what countries these DACA participants represent in each state? I would guess mostly Mexico and Central America, but I'm sure other countries must be represented as well. Possibly Cuba, Middle Eastern countries, South America,  African countries, and Asia? I wonder if the decline in the older age of entry is because older children are already established in their country of residence and it makes it harder for them to pack up and leave?

## 1) Chart type
A **composite visualization** combining:
- **Two horizontal bar charts** at the top
- **One tabular heatmap / highlighted table** at the bottom

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **multi-panel layout**:
  - Left panel: horizontal bars by **state**
  - Right panel: horizontal bars by **age at entry**
  - Bottom panel: **table** of occupations with two numeric columns
- No stacking is used.
- No faceting in the strict repeated-scale sense, but it functions as **separate panels/small sections** for different variables.
- Color highlighting is used to emphasize selected values/cells.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Row position / y-position in left horizontal bar chart; text label |
| DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in left chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Age at entry | Ordinal (discrete numeric categories shown as ages 0–15) | Row position / y-position in right horizontal bar chart; text label |
| Percent of DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in right chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Occupation | Categorical/nominal | Row position in bottom table; text label |
| DACA-eligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in left numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| DACA-ineligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in right numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| Highlight/emphasis status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (yellow vs blue in bars; shaded cells in table) |

## 1) Chart type
A **composite visualization** combining:
- **Two horizontal bar charts** at the top
- **One tabular heatmap / highlighted table** at the bottom

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **multi-panel layout**:
  - Left panel: horizontal bars by **state**
  - Right panel: horizontal bars by **age at entry**
  - Bottom panel: **table** of occupations with two numeric columns
- No stacking is used.
- No faceting in the strict repeated-scale sense, but it functions as **separate panels/small sections** for different variables.
- Color highlighting is used to emphasize selected values/cells.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Row position / y-position in left horizontal bar chart; text label |
| DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in left chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Age at entry | Ordinal (discrete numeric categories shown as ages 0–15) | Row position / y-position in right horizontal bar chart; text label |
| Percent of DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in right chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Occupation | Categorical/nominal | Row position in bottom table; text label |
| DACA-eligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in left numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| DACA-ineligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in right numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| Highlight/emphasis status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (yellow vs blue in bars; shaded cells in table) |

## 1) Chart type
A **composite visualization** combining:
- **Two horizontal bar charts** at the top
- **One tabular heatmap / highlighted table** at the bottom

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **multi-panel layout**:
  - Left panel: horizontal bars by **state**
  - Right panel: horizontal bars by **age at entry**
  - Bottom panel: **table** of occupations with two numeric columns
- No stacking is used.
- No faceting in the strict repeated-scale sense, but it functions as **separate panels/small sections** for different variables.
- Color highlighting is used to emphasize selected values/cells.

|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Row position / y-position in left horizontal bar chart; text label |
| DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in left chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Age at entry | Ordinal (discrete numeric categories shown as ages 0–15) | Row position / y-position in right horizontal bar chart; text label |
| Percent of DACA beneficiaries | Quantitative | Bar length in right chart; numeric label inside/near bars |
| Occupation | Categorical/nominal | Row position in bottom table; text label |
| DACA-eligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in left numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| DACA-ineligible workers | Quantitative | Numeric text in right numeric column of table; cell background highlight/color intensity |
| Highlight/emphasis status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (yellow vs blue in bars; shaded cells in table) |
